articles.title: Cellular senescence in ageing and neurodegenerative disorders: Molecular mechanisms, biomarkers, and therapeutic strategies.
articles.abstract: Cellular senescence has been increasingly associated with neurodegenerative disorders, potentially linking ageing-related cellular impairment with mitochondrial dysfunction, chronic inflammation, and disrupted intercellular signalling. The present study aims to explore the increasing relevance of cellular senescence among key cell types, including neurons, astrocytes, neural progenitor cells, microglia and oligodendrocyte-lineage cells across neurodegenerative ailments such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and multiple sclerosis. This review discusses the findings of pre-clinical and clinical studies which suggest that senescence-associated features may contribute to neurodegeneration. Further, it provides an overview of the biomarkers used in the identification of senescence in the CNS. Also, the review examines senotherapeutic treatment approaches, highlighting their actions on different CNS cell types and the growing clinical evidence. It also points out the challenges in translating these approaches to clinical application, such as targeting specific cell types and the lack of suitable biomarkers. Collectively, present findings suggest that senescence-associated alterations may contribute to neurodegeneration, although their effects appear to vary across cell types and diseases.

articles.title: Drosophila Models of Human Neurodegenerative Diseases.
articles.abstract: In his book Insects and the Life of Man: Collected Essays on Pure Science and Applied Biology, Sir V. B. Wigglesworth examined how a fundamental understanding of insect physiology and biology can be applied to some of society's greatest challenges, including human health. Here we reflect on how, in the 50 years since his book's publication, Drosophila melanogaster have played a critical role in advancing our understanding of human neurodegenerative diseases. Focusing on Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, and the frontotemporal dementia / amyotrophic lateral sclerosis spectrum, we examine the role Drosophila have played in elucidating fundamental mechanisms of neurodegeneration, identifying therapeutic targets, and dissecting the complex interplay that exists between genetics and environmental factors. Together these studies highlight how Drosophila models continue to provide critical insight into the molecular mechanisms underpinning neurodegeneration and provide a fundamental pre-clinical model in which we can accelerate research into human neurodegenerative conditions.

articles.title: Mitochondrial dysfunction in neurology: biomarkers and clinical implications.
articles.abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction is increasingly recognized as a shared downstream pathogenic mechanism across a wide spectrum of neurological disorders, ranging from primary mitochondrial diseases to conditions including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease, multiple sclerosis, hereditary ataxias and idiopathic inflammatory myopathies. This Review examines the role of mitochondrial biomarkers in improving diagnostic accuracy, patient stratification and monitoring of disease progression and therapeutic response. Primary mitochondrial diseases are presented as proof-of-concept models of impaired oxidative phosphorylation, providing a framework for biomarker identification and validation with translational relevance to other neurological diseases. Mitochondrial biomarkers can be broadly categorized into four domains: fluid biomarkers, reflecting metabolic alterations and stress signalling; genetic biomarkers, capturing mitochondrial DNA integrity and dynamics; multi-omics approaches, integrating transcriptomic, proteomic and metabolomic signatures; and imaging biomarkers, enabling in vivo assessment of structural and functional consequences of mitochondrial dysfunction. Across disorders, these biomarkers reveal shared disturbances in bioenergetics, redox homeostasis, mitochondrial genome maintenance and inflammatory signalling. However, clinical implementation remains limited by methodological heterogeneity, biological variability and reduced disease specificity. Integrated, multimodal biomarker strategies, combined with longitudinal validation, will be essential for supporting precision medicine and guiding the development of therapies to target mitochondrial pathways in neurology.

articles.title: Neurodegeneration in Sub-Saharan Africa: Intersections of Biological Ageing, Genomic Diversity and the Lifetime Exposome.
articles.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases are emerging as an important consequence of population ageing in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), but their scientific relevance extends beyond a projected rise in case numbers. SSA combines exceptional human genomic diversity with marked heterogeneity in vascular and metabolic risk, infection, nutrition, occupational exposures, air pollution, and access to health care. This combination creates an underused setting in which to study why biological ageing produces neurodegeneration in some individuals but relative resilience in others. This review critically synthesises evidence on Alzheimer's disease and related dementias, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis/frontotemporal degeneration, Huntington's disease and related disorders, focusing on the intersection between hallmarks of ageing, disease-specific proteinopathies, ancestry and the lifetime exposome. Age-associated loss of proteostasis, mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired autophagy, chronic inflammation, neurovascular injury and genomic/epigenomic instability provide a mechanistic scaffold on which genetic susceptibility and cumulative exposures may act. Yet African evidence remains dominated by cross-sectional clinical phenotyping; neuropathology, longitudinal biomarkers, multi-omics and measured environmental exposures remain sparse. Recent African-ancestry Parkinson's disease genomics and emerging plasma biomarker studies demonstrate that ancestry-inclusive molecular neuroscience is feasible and can generate findings not predictable from European-ancestry datasets. The next phase should therefore move beyond documenting underdiagnosis toward longitudinal, biologically anchored cohorts that integrate phenotype, genomics, blood biomarkers, neuroimaging, exposomics, digital measures and health-system outcomes. This review proposes a research framework centred on biological ageing, gene-environment interaction and resilience. Such work would improve the validity of prevention, diagnosis and therapeutic translation in African populations while contributing globally to a more complete biology of neurodegenerative ageing.

articles.title: State transitions in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis: mechanistic convergence and biomarker-guided stratification.
articles.abstract: Biological heterogeneity is a major obstacle to therapeutic development in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Cross-sectional pathway labels do not show whether a mechanism is active or treatment-relevant in an individual patient. We conducted a structured critical narrative review informed by the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles. MEDLINE, Embase, PubMed, and CENTRAL were searched for English-language literature published from 1 January 2015 to 7 August 2026; seminal earlier studies were identified by citation tracking. Human genetic, pathological, longitudinal biomarker, multi-omic, imaging, neurophysiological, and interventional evidence was prioritized. Evidence was appraised by human proximity, temporality, replication, mechanistic specificity, and treatment relevance. Evidence supports interacting RNA/proteostasis, nucleocytoplasmic-transport, glial-inflammatory, and energetic-metabolic processes, but current evidence does not yet support the use of any candidate state for individual treatment assignment. The most mature temporal example is loss of TDP-43 splicing repression before neurofilament elevation in genetically at-risk individuals. Nucleocytoplasmic-transport evidence is strongest in C9orf72 disease; inflammatory and metabolic signals are confounded by disease burden and systemic illness; and the gut-brain axis remains a context-dependent amplifier. We propose prespecified transition rules, evidence grades, and biomarker-by-treatment interaction tests. A state-transition model becomes clinically useful when longitudinal measurements add value beyond clinical predictors and injury markers and prospectively identify differential treatment benefit.

articles.title: Clinically unresponsive patients with acute brain injury activate a brain-computer interface.
articles.abstract: Brain activation to verbal commands can be detected by EEG in clinically unresponsive patients. These patients with cognitive motor dissociation (CMD) are unable to communicate with the environment despite preserved consciousness. Advanced brain-computer interfaces (BCI) are promising to support motor function in patients with motor neuron disease or spinal cord injury. Our primary objective was to determine if clinically unresponsive patients can control a self-paced, one-way BCI early after acute brain injury. Secondarily, we assessed the association of BCI control with short- and long-term outcomes. We conducted a prospective single-centre cohort study in 41 clinically unresponsive, critically ill and acutely brain injured patients, as well as in a convenience sample of 8 healthy volunteers and 22 conscious critically ill patients. The self-paced BCI analysed EEG in real time and modulated frequency and pitch of a tone that patients controlled by attempting a motor task: patients were provided with instructions 'to make the beep sound faster, keep opening and closing your right hand' alternating with 'to make the beep sound slower, stop opening and closing your right hand'. CMD was detected by applying machine learning to EEG recorded while patients listened to motor commands. Clinical outcomes were recovery of consciousness by hospital discharge, assessed with the Coma Recovery Scale-Revised, and recovery of functional independence at 12 months, defined as a Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended score of 4 or higher (denoting the ability to function independently for 8 h or more). Additionally, we invited conscious patients as well as family members of conscious and clinically unresponsive patients to complete a survey on perceived utility and challenges associated with the BCI. In this study, 13 clinically unresponsive patients (32%) achieved BCI control and 8 of 41 (20%) were CMD-positive. All healthy volunteers and nine conscious patients (41%) were able to control the BCI. Median signal delay for BCI control was 49.8 [interquartile range (IQR) 39.9-75.6] seconds for clinically unresponsive patients, 17.1 (IQR 7.8-19.9) for conscious patients and 15.5 (IQR 12.9-21.2) for healthy volunteers. In the group of 41 clinically unresponsive patients, 4 of 13 patients with (31%) and 1 of 28 without BCI control (4%) recovered clinical consciousness at hospital discharge [odds ratio (OR) 21.2; 95% confidence interval (CI) 2.3-930.7]. At 12 months, 6 of 13 patients with (46%) and 2 of 28 without BCI control (7%) recovered functional independence (OR 9.9; 95% CI 1.8-81.6). None of the patients that were unable to control the BCI and were CMD-negative recovered. Patients with BCI control had shorter times to recovery of functional independence by 12 months than those who did not (hazards ratio 6.0; 95% CI 1.2-30.6). All respondents of the BCI survey (n = 37) expressed strong support for the potential future use of BCI devices. These results suggest that BCI control is a strong predictor of outcomes following acute brain injury and provide initial evidence that a bedside, EEG-based BCI system might permit bidirectional communication in critically ill unresponsive patients.

articles.title: Tau isoform mapping across tissues and biofluids reveals a signature distinguishing Alzheimer's disease from amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
articles.abstract: Blood phosphorylated tau 217 (p-tau217) accurately detects Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology but is also elevated in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), likely reflecting peripheral (big) tau released from muscle. Assays selectively measuring brain-derived (BD-) tau and BD-p-tau217 are therefore needed. We analysed serum BD-tau and p-tau217 in ALS (n = 139), AD (n = 101) and controls (n = 75) using direct immunoassays and after BD-Tau immunoprecipitation (BD-Tau-IP), and tau species in brain (n = 16), spinal cord (n = 11) and muscle (n = 10) by targeted mass spectrometry. With the direct immunoassays, BD-tau and p-tau217 were increased in AD and ALS versus controls. After BD-Tau-IP, BD-tau and BD-p-tau217 were elevated in AD only, improving diagnostic accuracy. Mass spectrometry revealed a central-to-peripheral shift from BD-tau to big tau predominance, with exclusively big p-tau217 detected in muscle. Selective detection of BD-tau species improves the specificity of blood AD biomarkers by reducing peripheral tau confounding.

articles.title: Cold activates a BH2 metabolic network promoting longevity and proteostasis.
articles.abstract: Moderately cold temperatures extend lifespan and promote health across species 1-3 , yet the molecular mechanisms underlying these benefits remain unclear. Here we define a metabolite-driven, multi-tissue signalling system that links cold temperature to enhanced longevity and proteostasis in Caenorhabditis elegans. Cold temperature upregulates the biopterin-synthesis enzyme CAT-4 (GCH1 in humans), increasing production of dihydrobiopterin (BH2), a transportable reservoir for the bioactive cofactor tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4). BH2 is produced in muscle and transported to distal tissues, including the intestine and neurons, where it is converted into BH4 by the salvage enzyme DHFR-1. BH4 functions as an essential cofactor for phenylalanine hydroxylase PAH-1, promoting tyrosine synthesis and extending lifespan. This BH2-BH4 axis also prevents disease-related protein aggregation and subsequent neuronal dysfunction during ageing. Importantly, increasing BH2 synthesis specifically in muscle is sufficient to promote longevity and suppress pathological protein aggregation in distal tissues, even at normal or elevated temperatures. In human cells, BH2 or tyrosine supplementation reduces aggregation of polyQ-expanded proteins associated with Huntington's disease, as well as mutant variants of TDP-43 and FUS that cause amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Together, these findings identify BH2 as a cold-induced metabolite of which the synthesis, intertissue transport and conversion into bioactive BH4 preserve organism-wide proteostasis and extend lifespan.

articles.title: Cytoplasmic TDP-43 Accumulation in Autosomal Recessive Spastic Ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay.
articles.abstract: Autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay (ARSACS) is a rare, early-onset neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive cerebellar ataxia, spasticity and peripheral neuropathy. It is caused by biallelic mutations in the SACS gene, which encodes sacsin, a large protein involved in cytoskeletal organization and mitochondrial homeostasis, and protein quality control. Despite advances in understanding sacsin biology, the molecular mechanisms underlying neurodegeneration in ARSACS remain incompletely understood. Here, we report the first neuropathological evidence of pathological TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) accumulation in ARSACS. Available postmortem brain tissue from a genetically confirmed ARSACS patient homozygous for the Quebec founder mutation ( SACS c.8844delT) was analyzed by immunohistochemistry, immunofluorescence and biochemical fractionation. Neurons in the prefrontal cortex, motor cortex and cerebellum exhibited cytoplasmic phosphorylated dot-like TDP-43 (pTDP-43) aggregates with reduced nuclear localization. Biochemical fractionation further identified detergent-insoluble TDP-43 species in ARSACS tissue. Additional pathological features included increased neurofilament accumulation, vacuole-like neuronal changes, Purkinje cell loss and p62-positive cytoplasmic inclusions. Similar dot-like cytoplasmic pTDP-43 aggregates were observed in a second ARSACS case. These findings identify pTDP-43 as a previously unrecognized pathological feature of ARSACS. While the patient exhibited no clinical or histopathological signs of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, the presence of atypical pTDP-43 aggregates observed in ARSACS may represent a rare, secondary, early-stage or potentially underrecognized manifestation of TDP-43 pathology rather than a defining hallmark of the disease. Further studies in additional patients and experimental ARSACS models will be required to determine the prevalence and mechanistic basis of TDP-43 abnormalities in this disorder.

articles.title: End-of-life care of patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and home mechanical ventilation: the national population-based DISCOVERY study.
articles.abstract: Background: Home mechanical ventilation (HMV), including noninvasive ventilation (NIV) and invasive ventilation (IV), is increasingly used in people with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (pwALS), but its impact on end-of-life care remains unclear. Objective: To examine whether ventilation pathway (NIV or IV) influences symptom prevalence and relief during the final week of life in pwALS. Secondary objectives were to assess end-of-life discussions, place and cause of death, and anticipated death. Methods: This national, population-based retrospective cohort study included pwALS using HMV in the Swedish National Quality Registry for Respiratory Failure (Swedevox), cross-linked with the Swedish Register of Palliative Care, which contains staff-reported end-of-life data, and other national registries. Results: Among 652 pwALS, 609 received NIV (mean age 66 years, 42% female) and 43 IV (mean age 60 years, 42% female). Anxiety and breathlessness were more common in the NIV group (76% vs 48% and 72% vs 31%, both p < 0.001), while prevalence and relief of other symptoms were similar between groups. Most patients had end-of-life discussions (NIV 87%, IV 92%). NIV patients more often died in specialized palliative wards (22% vs 7%, p = 0.023). Most deaths were due to ALS (96%) and were anticipated (NIV 94%, IV 88%). Conclusions: In pwALS with HVM, NIV was associated with higher rates of anxiety and breathlessness in the final week of life, but the ventilation pathway did not influence overall symptom relief. End-of-life communications and cause of death were similar; place of death differed by ventilation pathway; however, most deaths were anticipated.

articles.title: Molecular signatures of selective motor neuron vulnerability in old age.
articles.abstract: Motor neuron (MN) death and impairment of fast-fatigable motor units is widely recognized in elderly humans and rats. However, the molecular signatures identifying vulnerable MNs remains underexplored. In murine models of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, matrix metalloproteinase 9 (MMP-9) and chondrolectin (Chodl) decline with disease progression and have been considered molecular markers of fast-fatigable MNs. However, their expression in brainstem and lumbar MNs, in accordance with the 'size principle' (in which motor units are recruited in a size-dependent manner, with MNs of lower capacitance activated before those of greater capacitance) and their expression throughout the lifespan remain unclear. Here, we evaluated MMP-9 and Chodl in lumbar and hypoglossal MNs in young (6 months) and old (24 months) Fischer 344 (F344) rats. Longitudinal lumbar spinal cord transverse brainstem sections (the orientations providing maximal MN somal sizes for each pool) were immunolabelled for choline acetyltransferase, MMP-9 and Chodl. Expression was quantified using confocal microscopy in young and old rats (n = 5 females, n = 5 males per age). Overall, MMP-9 demonstrated a positive association with lumbar MN somal surface area in young rats. Paired within-animal analysis showed that in larger MNs, MMP-9 positivity was ∼70% greater than smaller MNs. The size-dependence of MMP-9 expression was absent in old lumbar MNs, suggesting either selective loss or downregulation of MMP-9 MN expression in ageing. No size-dependent change in Chodl was observed in lumbar or hypoglossal MNs, nor was MMP-9 associated with MN size in hypoglossal MNs. Collectively, these findings identify MMP-9 as a marker enriched within large lumbar MNs in young rats and suggest that age-related alterations in MMP-9 expression may reflect the selective vulnerability of the lumbar MNs.

articles.title: Neurotransmitter-defined cerebral vulnerability patterns in frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD).
articles.abstract: Frontotemporal dementia syndromes encompass a genetically, clinically and radiologically heterogeneous set of conditions with distinctive clinical and imaging characteristics. The main FTD phenotypes exhibit strikingly different disease burden patterns with a predilection to specific brain regions and relative sparing of others. The apparent selectivity of cerebral involvement in FTD has not been fully elucidated. A prospective neuroimaging study has been undertaken with a uniform imaging protocol to characterise atrophy patterns in ALS-FTD, behavioural variant FTD, nonfluent variant primary progressive aphasia, and semantic variant primary progressive aphasia and evaluate associations with physiological neurotransmitter receptor expression maps. Anatomical correlations between focal volume loss and a large panel of neurotransmitters were systematically evaluated and associations ranked. Associations were noted with GABAergic, opioid, cannabinoid, microglial and acetylcholine systems in ALSFTD-C9NEG. Correlations were observed with opioid, glutaminergic, and synaptic vesicle glycoprotein 2A receptor populations in ALSFTD-C9POS. Atrophy in bvFTD showed predilection to serotonergic, glutaminergic, opioid, GABAergic and cannabinoid circuits. Volume loss in nfvPPA colocalised with GABAergic, opioid, microglial, serotonergic, cannabinoid, acetylcholine, glutaminergic and dopaminergic networks. A multitude of neurotransmitter populations are implicated in svPPA including opioid, serotonergic, GABAergic, dopaminergic, and microglial systems. The distinctive neuroimaging signatures of FTD phenotypes exhibit spatial associations with physiological neurotransmitter receptor density maps. The propensity of atrophy to specific brain regions in FTD subtypes may be defined by neurotransmitter populations. Our findings indirectly support the notion of neurotransmitter-system defined connectivity-based disease propagation in FTD.

articles.title: Serum p-tau181 and p-tau217 levels in adolescents and adults with 5q spinal muscular atrophy.
articles.abstract: Reliable blood biomarkers for longitudinal monitoring in adolescent and adult 5q spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) are lacking. Phosphorylated tau (p-tau) species are elevated in serum in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), where they may reflect peripheral nerve and muscle pathology. We aimed to investigate serum p-tau181 and p-tau217 as longitudinal biomarkers in adolescent and adult SMA and assessed associations with clinical parameters. In this retrospective multi-centre study, we assessed serum p-tau181 and p-tau217 levels in adults with 5q SMA under treatment with nusinersen or risdiplam, comparing levels with Alzheimer's disease (AD), amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and non-neurodegenerative disease controls. Associations with motor function, respiratory capacity, creatine kinase (CK), and neurofilament light chain (NfL) were assessed using linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age and sex. Serum p-tau181 was higher in SMA than in disease controls (β = -0.48, 95%-CI -0.81 to -0.15), but lower than in ALS (β = 0.99, 95%-CI 0.58 to 1.39) and AD (β = 0.56, 95%-CI 0.11 to 1.00). P-tau181 declined from baseline to FUP2 (Δ median -1.80 pg/mL, IQR -5.90 to 2.10); p-tau217 showed no longitudinal change. P-tau181 and p-tau217 were positively associated with motor function, functional status, respiratory capacity, and CK, with no association with NfL. In exploratory analyses, higher baseline p-tau181 was associated with greater HFMSE decline (β = 1.79, 95%-CI 0.59 to 2.99). Serum p-tau181 and p-tau217 appear to reflect ongoing muscle turnover in adult SMA, declining as muscle mass decreases. Higher baseline p-tau181 was associated with subsequent functional deterioration, suggesting potential utility as a biomarker of active denervation and disease monitoring.

articles.title: Towards semantic brain-computer interfacing: The graded inventory of semantic triggers (GIST) paradigm.
articles.abstract: Semantic Brain-Computer Interfaces (sBCIs) aim to decode conceptual information directly from neural activity, enabling more efficient and natural communication for individuals with severe motor impairments. However, existing approaches are often confounded by stimulus-driven perceptual processes and lack a reliable means of tagging the moment of concept formation. We introduce the Graded Inventory of Semantic Triggers (GIST), a novel electroencephalography (EEG) paradigm designed to elicit semantic retrieval from graded verbal clues with precise temporal alignment.Approach: EEG data were recorded from 14 participants performing the GIST task across three semantic categories (food, musical instruments, and body parts). Target neural activity was aligned to each participant's self-reported moment of semantic retrieval (spacebar press), enabling response-locked analysis. Here, we propose a staged framework where the first comprises a Conformer-based encoder trained on pooled data using a hybrid contrastive objective that combines instance-level consistency and cross-participant class alignment with domain-adversarial learning to reduce participant-specific information. In the second stage, the frozen encoder is transferred to a held-out participant whose data played no part in Stage 1, and a support vector machine is calibrated on that participant's own labelled items under a nested leave-one-item-out protocol.Results: Above-chance semantic decoding was achieved in all three pairwise tasks. Mean accuracies were 73.4% (Body vs. Food), 70.7% (Body vs. Music), and 68.2% (Food vs. Music). Participant-level permutation tests were significant in 9/11 participants for Body vs. Food and 8/11 for each of the other tasks (p < 0.05). The pre-response interval at [-1.5s, -0.5s] was the most discriminative.Significance: The GIST paradigm enables controlled elicitation and temporal alignment of semantic processing while reducing perceptual confounds. Combined with cross-participant representation pretraining and participant-specific calibration, the results demonstrate above-chance decoding of semantic categories from EEG in individuals excluded from representation learning, supporting the feasibility of sBCIs.

articles.title: Understanding Holistic Patient-Relevant Measurement in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis: A Mixed-Methods Content Validity and Exploratory Rasch Analysis of Selected Clinical Outcome Assessments.
articles.abstract: Living with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) has a profound impact on function and health-related quality of life (HRQoL). This mixed-methods study aimed to cognitively debrief selected ALS outcome measures to investigate their relevance and conduct exploratory Rasch Measurement Theory (RMT) analyses to assess targeting. Semi-structured interviews were conducted (January-September 2024) with people living with ALS (PLwALS) and clinicians to cognitively debrief selected patient- and clinician-reported outcome (PRO and ClinRO) measures. The PRO measures debriefed with PLwALS were Rasch Overall ALS Disability Scale (ROADS), 5-item ALS Assessment Questionnaire (ALSAQ-5), and Neurological Fatigue Index for Motor Neurone Disease (NFI-MND). ROADS and ClinRO ALS Functional Rating Scale-Revised (ALSFRS-R) were debriefed with clinicians. Interview transcripts were qualitatively analyzed; structured codes were used to compile data on item relevance and comprehensiveness. Exploratory RMT analysis was conducted using quantitative data from PLwALS responses to evaluate selected PRO psychometric properties. Qualitative analysis of interviews with 31 PLwALS found that PROs were meaningful and relevant, and identified the relevance of individual items. Clinicians (n = 10) endorsed ALSFRS-R as a relevant and meaningful measure, and supported ROADS' conceptual coverage and response category. RMT analysis indicated evidence of good targeting, reliability, and item fit for the PROs, with some exceptions for ALSAQ-5. This study supports the use of ALSFRS-R, ROADS, ALSAQ-5, and NFI-MND to measure meaningful aspects of ALS, with support for ALSAQ-5 qualified by its limited measurement precision. Scores from these measures can provide important insights into the lived experience of PLwALS, characterizing disease progression and HRQoL.

articles.title: "It's like saving for a rainy day": perceptions of voice banking for people living with Motor Neurone Disease.
articles.abstract: This exploratory qualitative study examined how people living with Motor Neurone Disease (PlwMND) and their partners perceived voice banking and related voice preservation counseling within a specialist Australian service. Semi-structured interviews were conducted in 2022 with five PlwMND and two partners. Participants represented varying levels of engagement with voice banking, including individuals who had completed voice banking and those who had not commenced and therefore discussed voice banking conceptually. Participants described voice banking as a means of preserving identity and social connection, while also identifying uncertainty about timing, emotional readiness, and the practical demands of early action. Variable clinician knowledge, service navigation challenges, and confusion between voice preservation methods highlight the importance of informational counseling experiences. Findings are interpreted as reflections of participant perceptions at a specific point in time and within a single service context, rather than evaluations of current technological capability. The study highlights the importance of proactive, accurate, and staged informational counseling that reflects evolving voice preservation technologies and local service pathways.

articles.title: ABCD-Trial: study protocol for a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study in patients with Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis for the evaluation of efficacy and safety of B-Cell Depletion with rituximab (ABCD).
articles.abstract: The exact disease-causing mechanisms in ALS remain incompletely understood. A possible cause is inflammation of neurons. Compared to other neurodegenerative diseases, neuroinflammation is pronounced in ALS, presumably leading to disease progression and neuronal death. Patients with ALS can have neuronal autoantibodies and most notably antibody-producing cells in the cerebrospinal fluid. The CD20-binding therapeutic antibody rituximab targets these antibody-producing B-cells. Rituximab is a medication commonly used in neurology. Single patients with ALS have already been treated with rituximab, which was well tolerated. We therefore want to evaluate safety and efficacy of a treatment with rituximab in ALS patients in a double-blind placebo-controlled trial. With this trial we aim for slower disease progression and unveiling disease-causing mechanisms in ALS. A total of 52 male and female patients older than 18 years with active sporadic ALS and disease duration of less than 24 months who are on a stable dose of riluzole (50 mg BID) should be included. Patients requiring assisted ventilation of any kind or have a known intolerance to the study medication rituximab are excluded. The study medication rituximab or placebo should be administered over a period of 52 weeks at 4 distinct time points, followed by a follow-up period of 79 weeks with 4 visits. Treatment efficacy should be evaluated using the ALS functioning scale ALSFRS-R-SE at every study visit (except safety visits). Safety will be assessed through regular laboratory analyses, adverse event (AE) and serious adverse event (SAE) monitoring, and CD20+ B-cell kinetics. The primary endpoint is the change in the ALS Functional Rating Scale-Revised (ALSFRS-R-SE) from baseline to week 79. Trial sites will be at Charité/DZNE Berlin and DZNE Bonn. ALS is a rapidly progressive neurodegenerative disease with limited treatment options. Recent preclinical in vivo studies suggest that B-cell-mediated autoimmunity contributes to disease progression. This trial will evaluate whether rituximab, which specifically depletes CD20+ B-cells, can slow ALS progression and provide insights into disease mechanisms. The trial was registered in the German WHO-recognized primary register Deutsches Register Klinische Studien DRKS (German Clinical Trials Register) on 3/07/2023 under registration number DRKS00030948.

articles.title: Cerebrospinal fluid amyloid and neurodegeneration biomarkers in the diagnosis and prognosis of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis: a multicohort observational study.
articles.abstract: Neurofilament light chain (NfL) is an established biomarker for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). However, it remains unclear whether biomarkers reflecting amyloid-β metabolism (Aβ), tau (phosphorylated tau, pTau), and astrogliosis (glial fibrillary acidic protein, GFAP) can complement NfL in clinical applications. It is also unclear how Alzheimer's disease (AD) co-pathology affects disease progression in ALS. We studied 264 patients with ALS and 164 disease-control participants, analysing baseline cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) NfL, Aβ peptides, pTau181, pTau217, and GFAP. A two-step diagnostic strategy was examined in individuals with intermediate NfL values, using machine-learning models. Prognostic associations were evaluated using linear mixed-effects and Cox models adjusted for established predictors; survival was additionally examined in pooled analyses including an external ALS cohort (n = 153). Patients with ALS exhibited higher CSF NfL, Aβ38, Aβ40, Aβ42, pTau181, and pTau217 than controls, even within Aβ-negative subgroups. NfL discriminated ALS from controls with an AUC of 0.85 (0.82-0.88), which increased to 0.90 (0.88-0.92) in machine-learning models incorporating additional biomarkers. The machine-learning models maintained a high positive predictive value (0.90) for classifying cases with intermediate NfL values. Significant Aβ × NfL interactions were observed for longitudinal functional decline, and pooled survival analyses showed stronger associations between NfL and survival in the Aβ-positive ALS subgroup (14%) than in the Aβ-negative ALS subgroup (HR 4.02 [2.17-7.45] vs 1.62 [1.36-1.92]). Multiple biomarker assessments can reduce misclassification of individuals with intermediate NfL values. CSF Aβ positivity modified the association between baseline NfL and disease progression. Personalised diagnosis and prognosis based on fine-grained co-pathology evaluation may enhance clinical management of ALS. This study was primarily supported by JST SPRING (JPMJSP2125). A complete list of funding organisations is provided in Acknowledgements.

articles.title: Factors associated with post-tracheostomy survival in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis.
articles.abstract: To identify demographic and clinical factors associated with post-tracheostomy survival using three well-characterized cohorts of patients with Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS). ALS patients from the Piemonte and Valle d'Aosta ALS Register (PARALS) diagnosed between 1995-2019 interval who underwent tracheostomy were included. A multivariable Cox proportional hazards model was used to identify factors associated with post-tracheostomy survival. Significant findings were tested in two independent cohorts, the Emilia-Romagna Region ALS Register (ERRALS) and an incident ALS cohort from South Sardinia. A total of 449 patients from PARALS underwent tracheostomy during the study period, with a median post-tracheostomy survival of 16.3 months (IQR 4.0-45.0). Younger age at tracheostomy was associated with longer survival (HR 1.03 per one-year increase, 95%CI1.01-1.05, p = 0.001), as being married/cohabiting (HR 0.78, 95%CI0.61-0.98, p = 0.033), a longer diagnosis-to-tracheostomy interval (HR 0.84 per one-year increase, 95%CI0.79-0.90, p < 0.001) and a lower ALS Functional Rating Scale slope from onset to tracheostomy (HR 1.13 per one-unit increase, 95%CI1.03-1.25, p = 0.012). These associations were replicated in the independent cohorts, when data were available. Additionally, discharge to nursing homes was associated with poorer survival in the Sardinian cohort (HR 4.23, 95%CI2.49-7.19; p < 0.001), whereas a more recent year of tracheostomy was associated with longer survival in the ERRALS cohort (HR 0.95, 95%CI0.90-0.99; p = 0.019). We identified multiple factors associated with post-tracheostomy survival in ALS patients, encompassing clinical and demographic characteristics at tracheostomy as well as local factors influencing peri- and post-operative care. These findings may support decision-making and clinician-patient communication in the advanced stages of ALS.

articles.title: The calibration-to-accuracy mapping in P300 spellers does not transport across cohorts and was not restored by tested alignment or local recalibration.
articles.abstract: ObjectiveA calibration-derived score has been related to online P300-speller accuracy in the same session, always within the cohort measured. We evaluated whether a mapping from that score to expected accuracy transports to withheld cohorts.ApproachRetrospective secondary analysis of BigP3BCI 1.0.0, the largest evaluation of this relationship to date: 18 of 20 studies contributed 271 participants, 739 session-condition records, and 19,611 character selections. The predictor was a decoder's cross-validated discriminability on calibration epochs, one study withheld from development. Between-cohort variation was summarised by the random-effects standard deviation tau.Main ResultsThe association was positive in all 18 cohorts but varied widely (r 0.190 to 0.928; participant-level r = 0.714, p < 0.001), with 12 CIs excluding zero. Pooled estimation error was 0.098 (95% CI 0.091 to 0.107) against a benchmark of 0.146. Calibration did not transport: intercept tau 0.87 (unrepresented-cohort interval -1.97 to 1.85, log-odds); cohort-specific slopes varied more than tenfold (tau 0.43, interval 0.111 to 2.005). Neither alignment (signal- or score-space) nor either nonlinear boundary meaningfully reduced this heterogeneity. Local recalibration with up to 16 participants did not reliably improve on transporting; refitting both intercept and slope was significantly worse than transporting at the smallest sizes. Median time per selection, a stopping-rule proxy, accounted for 66% of between-cohort slope variance in meta-regression. The four ALS cohorts gave an uncorrected slope spread of 0.223, against 0.560 overall.SignificanceThe evaluated score is a classifier's cross-validated discriminability on each session's calibration data rather than the source studies' undocumented online decoder. That score reproducibly signals within-session accuracy, but its mapping to accuracy is cohort-specific and supports ranking sessions after local validation rather than reporting accuracy elsewhere. The four-cohort ALS subgroup appeared more homogeneous than the full archive, illustrating how conclusions about transportability from a small cohort set can be fragile.&#xD.

articles.title: The Role of Astrocytes in the Inflammatory Response in Neurodiseases.
articles.abstract: Astrocytes have emerged as central regulators of neuroinflammation, extending far beyond their traditional roles as structural and metabolic support cells. In neurological disorders, astrocytes undergo reactive remodeling that encompasses morphological, transcriptional, metabolic, and functional changes. Rather than fitting into a fixed A1/A2 dichotomy, reactive astrocytes exist along a disease-, region-, and stage-dependent continuum shaped by local pathology and intercellular crosstalk. This review summarizes how astrocytes contribute to neuroinflammatory processes in Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Huntington's disease, central nervous system injury, infection, multiple sclerosis, epilepsy, and autism spectrum disorder. We highlight convergent mechanisms, including cytokine and chemokine release, complement activation, glutamate and ion homeostasis disruption, oxidative stress, metabolic reprogramming, and blood-brain barrier regulation, while emphasizing disease-specific astrocytic programs. We further discuss astrocyte interactions with microglia, neurons, oligodendrocytes, endothelial cells, and peripheral immune cells, as well as key regulatory pathways, epigenetic remodeling, and lipid-dependent metabolic signaling. Finally, we evaluate current and emerging astrocyte-targeted therapeutic strategies, including metabolic modulation, receptor targeting, gene editing, nanodelivery, and gut-brain axis interventions. Defining functionally validated astrocyte states and developing biomarker-guided, stage-adaptive therapies may enable more precise intervention in neuroinflammatory and neurodegenerative diseases.

articles.title: Mapping care interventions for people living with motor neurone disease: a living evidence and gap map.
articles.abstract: Motor neurone disease (MND) is a debilitating, life-limiting neurodegenerative disease that has no cure. Caring for a person living with MND requires a multidisciplinary team delivering interventions to address symptoms. We aimed to map evidence supporting care of those living with MND. Evidence and gap maps (EGMs) were developed according to Campbell and JBI guidance for scoping reviews. Databases searched included CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and PsycINFO with no date restriction. Articles describing care interventions for people living with MND, carers, asymptomatic genetic carriers, family, friends, and healthcare professionals were included. 2390 reports were drawn from 1594 articles that were included across five EGMs, supportive and symptom management ( n = 673 articles), pharmacological ( n = 592), models of care ( n = 196), medical and clinical interventions ( n = 185), and technology and equipment ( n = 91). Interventions primarily addressed people who are living with MND ( n = 1732). No articles were identified specifically concerning First Nations Peoples, Culturally and Linguistically Diverse Peoples, or those living in remote, rural or regional areas. MND care interventions are diverse. Further research is needed to understand options for Culturally and Linguistically Diverse Peoples, First Nations Peoples, and those living in rural, regional, and remote communities.

articles.title: Protein disulphide isomerase protects against ALS/FTD phenotypes associated with cyclin F in zebrafish and cellular models.
articles.abstract: Mutations in CCNF , encoding cyclin F, cause a small proportion of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) cases. Mutant cyclin F mislocalises from the nucleus to the cytoplasm, impairs the ubiquitin proteasome system, disrupts endoplasmic reticulum (ER) to Golgi transport, and triggers ER stress and apoptosis. Protein disulphide isomerase (PDI), a redox-active ER chaperone of the thioredoxin superfamily, protects against ALS phenotypes induced by mutant SOD1, TDP-43, and FUS, but its activity against mutant cyclin F has not been examined. To test whether PDI overexpression prevents the cellular and behavioural phenotypes induced by the ALS/FTD-associated cyclin F S621G mutation. Neuro-2a cells were co-transfected with mCherry-tagged wild-type or mutant cyclin F S621G and V5-tagged PDI or empty vector. Subcellular localisation, XBP-1 and CHOP activation, proteasome reporter (GFPu) accumulation, nuclear morphology, and cleaved caspase-3 immunoreactivity were assessed by confocal microscopy. Transient transgenic zebrafish larvae generated by mRNA co-injection of cyclin F and PDI were assessed by photomotor response at 48 h post-fertilisation. Mutant cyclin F S621G induced cytoplasmic mislocalisation, ER stress (assessed by XBP-1 and CHOP activation), proteasome dysfunction (indicated by GFPu accumulation), and apoptosis (assessed by nuclear condensation and caspase-3 activation), all of which were significantly attenuated by PDI co-expression. Zebrafish larvae expressing cyclin F S621G swam significantly shorter distances than uninjected or wildtype controls, and co-expression of PDI restored motor function to near-wildtype levels. PDI protects against ALS/FTD-associated mutant cyclin F in both cellular and in vivo zebrafish models, identifying PDI as a redox-based therapeutic target for CCNF -linked ALS/FTD.
articles.journal: Redox report : communications in free radical research

articles.title: Cryo-EM advances in TDP-43 amyloid fibrils structure determination.
articles.abstract: TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) is a DNA/RNA-binding protein whose pathological aggregation characterizes a spectrum of neurodegenerative disorders known as TDP-43 proteinopathies, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD), and chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE). Recent breakthroughs in cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) have revolutionized our understanding of these diseases by resolving the atomic structures of TDP-43 amyloid fibrils. These structural insights have been pivotal in elucidating the transition from functional liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) to irreversible solid-state aggregation. This review synthesizes key cryo-EM findings from 2019 to 2026, encompassing fibrils formed by the full-length low-complexity domain, disease-relevant core fragments, and filaments extracted directly from patient tissues, as well as the pathological implications of distinct structural polymorphs. These findings not only deepen our understanding of the brain science aspects of the pathogenesis of TDP-43 proteinopathies, but also provide an important structural basis for the development of specific conformational diagnostic methods and targeted therapeutic drugs.

articles.title: Molecular recognition of axonal injury-associated candidate hub genes and predicted inhibitors across Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
articles.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) have converging molecular pathologies such as neuroinflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and axonal degeneration, but do not have broadly effective disease-modifying therapies. A novel computational strategy was used in this study with an integrated in-silico pipeline to determine common candidate hub genes across AD, PD, and ALS and to computationally screen candidate inhibitors. The gene expression datasets were retrieved from the Gene Expression Omnibus database and analyzed with limma R package for blood-derived gene expression datasets for AD (GSE63060), PD (GSE99039) and ALS (GSE112680). A multi-dataset intersection analysis revealed 138 genes commonly upregulated and 0 commonly downregulated genes, which were functionally enriched in immune regulation, apoptotic signaling and mitochondrial instability pathways. Protein-protein interaction network analysis identified three key genes (MMP9, PTPN6 and TNFRSF1A) as high-confidence candidate hub genes for AD, PD, and ALS. The ZINC library of 34,853 compounds was screened for drug-like properties using QikProp to yield 16,466 drug-like compounds. Based on the comparative screening results, the structure of MMP9 (PDB ID: 8K5Y) was chosen for further analysis and two of the selected compounds ZINC04582833, ZINC00047690 were identified as the two highest ranked compounds with docking scores of - 10.4 and - 9.7 kcal/mol respectively. Both complexes were further evaluated by 100 ns MD simulations, showing RMSD profile stability, maintained secondary structure for both complexes. The results in this study make ZINC04582833 and ZINC00047690 computationally prioritized candidates for shared neurodegenerative targets for experimental validation. The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s40203-026-00774-6.

articles.title: Peripheral and cerebrospinal fluid inflammatory markers in sporadic amyotrophic lateral sclerosis an exploratory cross-sectional association study.
articles.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder with an ambiguous etiology, whose onset may be linked to innate immune system activation outside the central nervous system (CNS). We investigated the association between peripheral blood and CNS inflammatory parameters in 45 sporadic ALS patients compared to 30 controls, analyzing peripheral blood tests (C-reactive protein [CRP], blood count, fibrinogen) and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) immunological measures (Tumor Necrosis Factor alpha [TNF-α], TNF receptor type 1 [TNFR-1], CRP) alongside clinical characteristics. Results revealed significantly higher concentrations of TNFR-1 in the CSF of ALS patients compared to the control group (1,029.5 ± 176.0 vs. 846.1 ± 167.5 pg/ml; p < 0.0001). This difference remained significant in multivariable logistic regression adjusting for age and sex (OR 1.82 per 100 pg/ml increment, 95% CI 1.26-2.63; p = 0.0015). In an exploratory ROC analysis, CSF TNFR-1 discriminated patients from controls with an AUC of 0.78 (95% CI 0.67-0.88). TNFR-1 correlated with age (R = 0.32, p = 0.038), associations with disease severity and a lower concentration in bulbar-onset disease were exploratory and not robustly significant. Plasma and CSF CRP concentrations did not differ significantly between groups, but strongly correlated with each other in both ALS (R = 0.83) and control (R = 0.82) cohorts, indicating a disease-non-specific relationship. CSF TNFR-1 is independently associated with sporadic ALS and warrants further investigation as a candidate disease-associated inflammatory biomarker. Given the limitations, our findings do not prove diagnostic accuracy or causality. Longitudinal studies with disease controls and blood-CSF barrier integrity measures are needed.
articles.journal: Neurological sciences : official journal of the Italian Neurological Society and of the Italian Society of Clinical Neurophysiology

articles.title: Restless legs syndrome and other neurological disorders: A systematic-narrative hybrid literature review with exploratory meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: Restless legs syndrome (RLS) is a sleep-related sensorimotor disorder affecting approximately 3% of adults worldwide. This review aims to synthesize current evidence on associations between RLS and major neurological conditions, provide an exploratory quantitative synthesis summarizing association patterns and heterogeneity, and identify priority mechanistic and clinical research gaps. Databases were searched from inception until August 2026. In our exploratory synthesis of 119 unique studies, RLS was significantly associated with Parkinson's disease (case-control OR 3.22, 95% CI 2.35-4.41; cohort RR 1.74, 95% CI 1.02-2.95), multiple sclerosis (OR 4.04, 95% CI 3.26-5.00), neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (OR 2.91, 95% CI 1.45-5.84), migraine or headache disorders (forward OR 2.72, 95% CI 2.19-3.38; reverse adjusted OR 1.53, 95% CI 1.36-1.73), peripheral neuropathy (OR 3.82, 95% CI 2.49-5.83), epilepsy (OR 2.11, 95% CI 1.58-2.82), and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (OR 7.69, 95% CI 2.74-21.59). This work is an evidence-mapping review with exploratory pooling and is not intended as a definitive evidence synthesis. RLS is likely associated with neurodegenerative and other specific neurological conditions. Recognition of these associations may support earlier identification of comorbid conditions and targeted management strategies. However, the current evidence remains observational and heterogeneous.

articles.title: Data-driven progression trajectories across clinical subtypes of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
articles.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) exhibits substantial clinical heterogeneity; however, conventional classifications based on the predominant site of involvement may not fully capture patterns of disease progression. This study aimed to identify data-driven subtypes of ALS and reconstruct their temporal progression using item-level scores from the ALS Functional Rating Scale-Revised (ALSFRS-R). Baseline data from 3067 participants in the Pooled Resource Open-Access ALS Clinical Trials database were analyzed. Subtype and Stage Inference (SuStaIn) was applied to ALSFRS-R item scores to identify subtypes and infer their progression trajectories. Internal consistency was evaluated using complexity and sensitivity analyses. Longitudinal stability was assessed at 180 and 365 days. Associations with functional decline and survival were examined using adjusted statistical models. Three clinically interpretable subtypes were identified, characterized by predominant upper-limb, lower-limb, or bulbar involvement. These subtypes exhibited distinct, consistent progression patterns across the analyses. Subtype stability was moderate short-term but limited longer-term; stage progression was largely monotonic. The bulbar subtype showed more rapid functional decline at both 180 and 365 days. Higher SuStaIn stage was associated with increased mortality. In an exploratory stage-stratified analysis, poorer survival was observed in the bulbar subtype than in the upper-limb subtype within the lower-stage group. This study reconstructed ALS subtype-specific functional progression trajectories and inferred disease stage using a widely accessible clinical scale. SuStaIn-derived subtypes characterized patterns of functional heterogeneity, and higher stage was associated with increased mortality. Further prospective comparative validation is needed to establish the prognostic and clinical utility of this framework.
authors: Pooled Resource Open-Access ALS Clinical Trials Consortium

articles.title: Registry Forge: an open-source end-to-end pipeline for patient-directed SMART on FHIR registries.
articles.abstract: Patient-directed SMART on FHIR lets registries acquire longitudinal electronic health record data, but the payload requires substantial engineering before use. We present Registry Forge, an open-source pipeline that converts it into curation-ready outputs. Registry Forge parses C-CDA, HTML, RTF, PDF, and FHIR inputs, joins records to a canonical identifier, and emits a browser dashboard, an OMOP CDM v5.4 data set, GA4GH Phenopackets v2, a code inventory, and disease-specific narrative extractions. Applied to the ALS Research Collaborative Study (94 participants, 56 US health systems), it processed 22 686 files and 1791 FHIR Bundles (109 599 resources); only 15.0% of files were full C-CDA XML; HTML (48.4%) and RTF (34.3%) predominated. Payloads are far more heterogeneous than often assumed; the architecture is designed for extension, though generalizability remains to be demonstrated. Registry Forge closes the gap between acquisition and curation-ready data with no server infrastructure and is openly available.

articles.title: Salivary Dim-Light Melatonin Onset is Associated with Functional Decline, Respiratory Symptom Emergence, and Survival in Early Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis.
articles.abstract: Sleep-wake and circadian disturbances are increasingly recognized in people living with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (plwALS), but endogenous circadian phase timing and its prognostic significance in early disease remain unclear. We assessed whether salivary dim-light melatonin onset (DLMO), an objective marker of central circadian phase, is altered in early plwALS and whether it provides prognostic information. In this prospective longitudinal observational study, plwALS within 18 months of symptom onset underwent home-based salivary melatonin sampling under dim-light conditions at 6 predefined time points around habitual sleep onset. Melatonin profiles were modeled using cubic smoothing splines, and DLMO was defined when the fitted curve first reached 3 pg/ml. Clinical, respiratory, and sleep assessments were collected at baseline (T0) and after 6 months (T6); a subgroup repeated saliva sampling at T6. Age- and sex-matched controls underwent melatonin profiling. Associations with disease progression, incident respiratory symptoms, and survival/tracheostomy were examined using regressions and survival analyses. A total of 50 plwALS were enrolled. Compared with controls, plwALS showed an earlier DLMO (20:24 ± 1:18 vs 20:58 ± 0:50; p = 0.028) despite similar habitual sleep onset and chronotype. Within ALS cohort, a later baseline DLMO correlated with worse functional/motor status, faster progression of disease, incident dyspnea/orthopnea by T6 (adjusted OR 3.11; p = 0.019), and poorer survival/tracheostomy-free outcome. In the resampled subgroup (n = 28), DLMO and melatonin-derived metrics did not change over ~6 months. Circadian phase alterations are detectable in early ALS. Baseline DLMO showed exploratory associations with functional, respiratory, and survival outcomes. Larger independent cohorts are required before DLMO can be considered a validated prognostic biomarker. ANN NEUROL 2026.
